newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: BPI says not to infuse more capital in PAL.
newsitem.headline: BPI says not to infuse more capital in PAL.

text.p: Bank of the Philippine Islands said on Tuesday it will not subscribe to a capital increase for Philippine Airlines Inc, effectively clearing the way for controversial tycoon Lucio Tan to expand his control of the troubled national carrier.
"We're just not convinced the reasons behind the capital hike will push through, given the track record of existing management," a BPI official told Reuters.
BPI, through its shares in PR Holdings which own 57 percent of PAL, has an equivalent stake of less than 7.0 percent in direct PAL shares.
Shareholders of the airline had been given a two-week deadline until Tuesday to subscribe to the capital increase.

At least two-thirds of the airline's stockholders agreed last September 10 to double the authorised capital stock to 10 billion pesos ($381.68 million) from 5.0 billion pesos ($190.84 million) to clear the way for an ambitious $4 billion re-fleeting programme.
BPI is owned by the Ayala family, one of the Philippines' traditional ruling families who frequently find themselves at odds with relative newcomers like Tan, who was born in China's Fujian province.
BPI had bitterly opposed Tan's efforts to take over the airline, which has been heavily losing money.
Tan is currently embroiled in a law suit with the government over tax evasion charges. He was a silent investor in PAL until he became chairman of PAL in 1994.
To date, the rest of the shareholders, except the government agencies, had agreed to subscribe to the PAL shares and pay the initial required capital, a PAL official said.
Among them, Aeropartners Corp, which represent investments of the Cojuangco group equivalent to 8.0 percent of the airline, has yet to pay the required capital, the official said.
Government agencies, which have direct and indirect minority PAL holdings, have already agreed to waive their pre-emptive rights to subscribe to the new shares in favour of Tan.
A PAL official said the government would still have the right of first refusal to take up BPI's preemptive rights. If it decides not to, then Lucio Tan can take up those shares.
The larger capital base of PAL is a prerequisite of creditors before giving more credit lines to PAL to funds its expansion programme.
"The new fleet will improve our on-time performance and safety," Tan said in a recent statement.
"We will be able to shed the 'plane-always-late' image and gain acceptance from more passengers. With all these, we expect to bring the airline back to profitability."
In the 1995/96 fiscal year ending March 31, PAL reported a net loss of 2.18 billion pesos ($83.21 million) against a 1.72 billion peso ($65.65 million) loss the previous year.
PAL's huge re-fleeting programme involves the acquisition of 36 new aircraft by the year 2000.
